stem: Atoms with nuclei containing an odd number of protons tend to have fewer isotopes than those with an even number of protons.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.stem: Gallium has two stable isotopes, $^{69}\text{Ga}$ and $^{71}\text{Ga}$.
parts.text:

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text:
The relative atomic mass of gallium, $A_{\text{r}}$, is 69.723.
The relative isotopic masses of $^{69}\text{Ga}$ and $^{71}\text{Ga}$ are:

$^{69}\text{Ga}$, 68.926; $^{71}\text{Ga}$, 70.925.

Use this information to calculate the percentage abundance of $^{69}\text{Ga}$ in elemental gallium.
Show your working.
Assume that the element contains only the $^{69}\text{Ga}$ and $^{71}\text{Ga}$ isotopes.
Give your answer to **four** significant figures.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.stem: Potassium also has two stable isotopes. Both isotopes have the same chemical properties.
parts.text: Explain why both isotopes of potassium have the same chemical properties.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: State the full electronic configuration of an atom of potassium.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
The first, second and third ionisation energies of potassium are 418, 3070 and $4600\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, respectively.

Use this information to explain why potassium is in Group 1.
